claims.text: Extending the dwell time at peak synthesis temperature improves atomic diffusion.
Improved diffusion from a longer peak-temperature dwell favors uniform single-phase solid-solution formation over phase separation.
Rapid heating and cooling of more-than-five-element noble-metal precursors typically yields inhomogeneous nanoparticles with localized phase separation and elemental segregation.
The controlled intervention is to extend only the peak-temperature dwell while retaining the rapid heating and cooling framework.
The applicable rapid thermal-processing timescale ranges from milliseconds to seconds.
The intervention applies to fixed multielement noble-metal precursors whose constituents have moderate differences in melting points and mixing enthalpies.
A longer dwell enhances local homogenization of nucleation centers and produces a more uniform elemental distribution.
Additional time at peak temperature allows atoms of different noble metals to overcome diffusion barriers.
Rapid cooling freezes in the structure established at high temperature.
Enhanced diffusion reduces local elemental clustering and suppresses secondary-phase nucleation or segregation.
Relative to the baseline cycle, extended dwell will produce a more uniform elemental distribution.
Relative to the baseline cycle, extended dwell will minimize phase segregation and yield a clearer single-phase solid-solution structure.
A very short thermal pulse of approximately 55 ms typically produces phase separation, elemental segregation, and variable particle morphology.
The hypothesis is most applicable when the constituent elements have relatively comparable diffusion characteristics.
Large disparities in melting points or mixing enthalpies may prevent adequate diffusion and homogenization even after extending the dwell.
The dwell-time extension needed to align diffusion timescales across dissimilar elements is unknown.
Precursor mobility restrictions and thermodynamic instabilities may also govern structure formation.

The dwell-time hypothesis is falsified if the extended-dwell samples show no statistically significant improvement in single-phase homogeneity or reductions in segregation relative to identically prepared baseline controls.
